title: Sustainability and Carbon Accounting

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Collecting Emissions Data
children.blurb: Collecting emissions data means gathering primary activity data and emission factors across scope 1, scope 2, and scope 3 categories for an organization or portfolio.

children.name: Checking Claims Against the Ledger
children.blurb: Checking claims against the ledger means comparing public sustainability and carbon statements, such as net zero pledges or emissions reductions, with the underlying accounting records and transactional data that support them.

children.name: Combining Financial and Non-Financial Data
children.blurb: Combining financial and non-financial data means bringing together traditional accounting figures, such as revenue, capital expenditure, and operating costs, with sustainability metrics like greenhouse gas emissions, water use, and workforce demographics.

children.name: Drafting Sustainability Disclosures
children.blurb: This page covers the use of AI to draft sustainability disclosures, including greenhouse gas emissions reports, climate risk narratives, and governance statements.

children.name: Carbon Credit Records
children.blurb: Carbon credit records are the structured documentation of verified emissions reductions or removals, including issuance, ownership, transfer, retirement, and any associated project data.

sections.body: This field covers how artificial intelligence handles emissions data, checks sustainability claims, combines financial and non-financial reporting, drafts disclosures, and records carbon credits. In practice, AI systems now read utility bills, supplier reports, and sensor feeds to assemble emissions inventories. They compare public statements against internal ledgers to flag mismatches. They also pull together accounting figures and environmental metrics into one dataset for reporting. The work is operational, not theoretical, and it runs on the same document and data processing tools used elsewhere in accounting.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Collecting emissions data is partly solved for scope 1 and 2 emissions where meters and invoices exist, but scope 3 data from suppliers remains messy and often estimated. Checking claims against a ledger works well for simple numeric mismatches, yet it struggles with vague language or off-balance-sheet commitments. Combining financial and non-financial data is technically possible but limited by inconsistent reporting standards and missing data. Drafting disclosures can produce competent first drafts, but a human still has to verify every material statement. Carbon credit records are only as reliable as the registries they draw from, and many credits are double counted or poorly verified. The honest limit is that AI can organize and flag, but it cannot make missing data appear or turn a weak claim into a true one.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader would start with Collecting Emissions Data to see how raw numbers enter the system. Then Checking Claims Against the Ledger shows how those numbers are tested against what a company has said. Combining Financial and Non-Financial Data explains the step where emissions figures meet accounting records, which is the core of integrated reporting. Drafting Sustainability Disclosures moves from data to narrative, showing how the assembled numbers become a report. Carbon Credit Records closes the loop by covering the offset instruments that many companies use to adjust their net figures. Together these pages follow the path from raw measurement to published disclosure and the credits behind it.
